strengths: Clear intuitive motivation with effective UMAP visualizations showing representation space trade-offs
Practical and elegant solution requiring only few lines of code, integrable into any OSR method without computational overhead
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 benchmarks (4 regular + 3 SSBs) and multiple OSR methods
Strong improvements on challenging semantic shift benchmarks (up to 3.56% AUROC gains)
Good reproducibility with provided code, detailed training specifications, and simple implementation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is reversing Kukleva et al. [2023]'s CosSch (k=0 to k=1), representing incremental modification rather than fundamental advance

Inconsistent improvements on regular benchmarks: negligible gains on CIFAR+50 (97.03% vs 97.03%), marginal on CIFAR10/CIFAR+10 (0.06-0.16%), with standard deviations often overlapping reported improvements
Method effectiveness highly scenario-dependent: significant performance only when training classes are large; acknowledged failure on small dataset benchmarks (CIFAR10, CIFAR+10, CIFAR+50)
Weak theoretical justification: no formal analysis of why NegCosSch is fundamentally superior to CosSch for OSR; reliance on intuition rather than principled argument
Hyperparameter sensitivity inadequately addressed: introduces three tunable parameters (τ+, τ-, P) with Figure 3 showing significant performance variance; no principled approach for setting P values
Incomplete comparison with closely related CosSch: main comparison relegated to appendix; improvements often marginal (0.22% on TinyImageNet, Table 4)
Statistical significance concerns: many improvements fall within reported standard deviations; no significance testing provided; CIFAR+50 shows 97.03%±0.23% for both methods
Variable performance across datasets unexplained: excellent on CUB but poor on Aircraft (Figure 4c shows negative improvements); suggests limited generalization
Unresolved interaction with label smoothing: Table 2 shows inconsistent synergy, indicating incomplete understanding of method
UMAP visualizations are qualitative: lack quantitative metrics (silhouette score, separation distance) to validate visual claims

strengths: Practical and simple method with zero computational overhead that can be easily integrated into any OSR approach with minimal code changes
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 datasets (4 standard + 3 semantic shift benchmarks) with multiple loss functions and baseline methods
Clear motivation and intuitive explanation supported by effective UMAP visualizations demonstrating the representation space evolution
Substantial improvements on harder semantic shift benchmarks (up to 3.56% AUROC and 4.32% OSCR), which are more realistic and challenging scenarios
Thorough reproducibility: extensive training details, hyperparameters, implementation code snippets, and promised code release
Good analysis showing benefits increase with training class count, suggesting the method helps where most needed (Figure 4)
Consistent improvements across multiple OSR methods (CE, SupCon, ConOSR, ARPL)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is reversing an existing scheduling direction from Kukleva et al. (2023); the generalization to GCosSch is straightforward
Inconsistent performance on standard benchmarks with marginal improvements (<0.1-0.3% AUROC on CIFAR benchmarks) and cases where CosSch outperforms NegCosSch (e.g., CIFAR+50)
Weak theoretical justification: explanations are intuitive but lack rigorous analysis; no formal justification for why k=1 is optimal or why this direction should preserve open set separation better
Method only benefits scenarios with more training classes and shows reduced or negative improvements with small number of classes (acknowledged but not addressed)
Incomplete hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: introduces new parameters (τ⁺, τ⁻, P) with limited exploration; guidance requires prior tuning of τ
Problematic interactions with label smoothing: negative performance in some cases (e.g., FGVC-Aircraft with SupCon + LS) without adequate explanation
Limited theoretical depth in understanding the representation geometry during scheduling and why the transition mechanism preserves open set separation
UMAP visualizations based on only 10 randomly chosen classes; no consistency checks across other datasets and limited exploration of alternative visualization methods
Incomplete failure analysis: Section 4.5 acknowledges limitations but doesn't investigate root causes or provide solutions
Most improvements on standard benchmarks appear marginal and may not be statistically significant; only Table 3 includes error bars

strengths: Clear and well-motivated analysis of temperature effects on representation learning (Section 3), explaining the trade-off between instance-level and semantic-level features with intuitive examples

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (CIFAR, TinyImageNet, semantic shift benchmarks), loss functions (CE, SupCon, ARPL), and metrics (accuracy, AUROC, OSCR) with proper ablation studies

Practical utility with zero computational overhead—the method integrates seamlessly into any temperature-dependent loss function, unlike prior OSR methods requiring auxiliary models or data augmentation
Strong improvements on harder semantic shift benchmarks with increasing number of training classes (Figure 3), showing the method addresses the tougher OSR scenarios
Excellent reproducibility: detailed training details, standard deviations across 5 seeds, implementation code provided, and promise of code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: temperature scaling and scheduling are well-established; the core contribution is reversing an existing cosine schedule (k=0 → k=1), making this feel incremental for a top-tier venue

Modest and inconsistent improvements: many gains are 1-2% within standard deviation ranges; clear failures exist (e.g., Aircraft SupCon+LS shows degradation; minimal CIFAR improvements); success seems context-dependent

Weak theoretical justification: the explanation that 'unknown samples stay distributed because features are unknown' is circular; why low-then-high temperature specifically helps OSR versus other scheduling patterns lacks rigor

Experimental setup concerns: paper uses different pretrained model for semantic shift benchmarks than prior work (Vaze et al. 2022, footnote 1), undermining direct comparison; baseline constant temperatures not thoroughly tuned

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance: heuristics like τ+ = τ + Δ (Δ ≈ 0.1-0.2) appear arbitrary; unclear how to select (τ+, τ-) for new problems; different rules for CE vs. SupCon loss unexplained
Limited analysis of failure cases and when the method does/doesn't work; minimal investigation into why CIFAR benchmarks show negligible gains or why Aircraft SupCon+LS degrades
Figure 1 UMAP visualizations are difficult to interpret—subtle visual differences make it hard to assess claimed representation quality improvements
